summary: `scheduleReconnect`'s timer dials unconditionally and only THEN assigns `this.ready`, so it never notices a dial another caller already started. `chargeDialAttempt` sets `nextDialAt = Date.now() + wait` and the `setTimeout(..., wait)` is armed a moment later, so the wall clock always crosses `nextDialAt` strictly before the timer can fire. Any `ensureUp()` landing in that window (core's 250 ms long-poll fallback, or a blocking `fetchRecent`) sees `ready === undefined` and `wait <= 0`, dials, and the ladder timer then dials a SECOND socket on top of it — two IDENTIFYs charged for one rung of the ladder that exists solely to ration the 1000/24h per-token quota whose penalty is a bot-token reset. The method's own comment claims the opposite ("a re-entrant caller (core's 250 ms long-poll fallback) cannot open a second socket alongside this one").
failure: Reproduced with a 20-line concrete subclass of `GatewayLadder` (counting dials, no `ws`): schedule a reconnect after a READY socket drops (jitter pinned to 0 ⇒ wait = 1000 ms), advance the system clock 1000 ms WITHOUT firing timers, call `ensureUp()` → dial #1; then fire the timer → dial #2. Observed `dials === 2`, expected 1. Second socket also installs itself as `this.ws`, orphaning the first (which is only closed on its next inbound frame) — and the orphan already spent its IDENTIFY.
remediation: In `GatewayLadder.ensureUp`, refuse to dial while the ladder owns the next dial: inside `if (this.ready === undefined)`, add `if (this.reconnectTimer !== undefined) throw new Error('Discord gateway dial refused: the reconnect ladder already owns the next dial');` before the `nextDialAt` check. Do NOT instead guard the timer body with `if (this.ready !== undefined) return;` — after a READY socket drops non-terminally the close handler leaves `this.ready` as a STALE RESOLVED promise, so that guard would stop the ladder reconnecting at all.
testUpgrade: CLASS: any ladder path that opens a socket without going through the one budget. Parameterize a table over (who initiates: ensureUp / reconnect timer / close handler) × (arrival offset relative to nextDialAt: -1 ms, 0, +1 ms, +50 ms) × (previous socket reached READY: yes/no), asserting `dials` after fully draining timers equals the number of ladder RUNGS charged (`reconnectAttempts` delta), not merely that it is bounded. Existing `gateway-budget.test.ts` 'Discord IDENTIFY budget, whoever dials' and gateway-reconnect.test.ts:722 'sustained flapping stays under QUOTA_PER_DAY' are too narrow: both drive time forward only through `advanceTimersByTimeAsync`, which fires the reconnect timer at exactly nextDialAt and therefore can never open the lateness window. The generator must move the clock independently of the timer queue (`vi.setSystemTime`).

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `this.reconnectTimer`, already the sole backing of the public `get reconnectPending()`, and `DiscordPlugin.subscribe`'s existing catch branch: `const ladder = this.gateway.reconnectPending ? 'the reconnect ladder is retrying' : 'no reconnect is scheduled'` — which prints the accurate message for the newly-thrown case. `fetchRecent`'s `try { await withDeadline(this.gateway.ensureUp(), blockMs) } catch { /* no socket → skip the wait */ }` already swallows it.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: an `ensureUp()` arriving after `nextDialAt` has passed but before the pending reconnect timer has fired — today it dials, now it throws a transient error and the ladder's own dial lands milliseconds later. Every other state is unchanged, because in that state `nextDialAt` is already in the future and `ensureUp` already threw 'backing off for another Xms'.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — I applied this exact edit and ran the whole package suite: 1020 passed, and the only failure was my own scratch repro's intermediate assertion (`expect(l.dials).toBe(1)` right after the re-entrant call), which was written to pin the buggy behaviour. The repro's terminal assertion (total dials == 1) passes with the fix.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It fixes the double-dial. remediationCheck.interleavings: (1) ensureUp at t=nextDialAt-ε → throws 'backing off', timer dials at t_fire: one dial. (2) ensureUp at t∈[nextDialAt, t_fire) → NOW throws on the new guard, timer dials: one dial (today: two). (3) two concurrent ensureUp callers in that window → both hit the new guard, neither dials. (4) ensureUp after the timer has fired and cleared `reconnectTimer` → `this.ready` is the timer's in-flight dial, so the memo path is taken: one dial. (5) `stop()`/`restart()` racing the guard → `stop()` clears `reconnectTimer` first, so a subsequent ensureUp dials normally under the fresh epoch.

summary: `newestWindow` builds `limit=${size}&before=${before}` with NO encoding, where `before` is `walked.at(-1)?.id` — a message id taken verbatim from the provider's response body. `hasUsableId` accepts any non-empty string, so the id is never constrained to digits. The sibling `windowSince` on line 43 does encode (`after=${encodeURIComponent(last ?? since)}`), so this is a one-sided hole in an otherwise deliberate defence. The threat is in scope for this package by its own choice: README line 58 says a plaintext `http://` `api_url` to a remote host is warned about and NOT refused, so a MITM on that path is an acknowledged deployment.
failure:
Reproduced against test/fake-discord.ts: seed a channel, `injectFault({status:200, rawBody: <a full 100-record page whose OLDEST record has id '900&limit=1&after=0'>})`, then `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 150})`. The fake logged the two requests it received:
  /api/v10/channels/900001/messages?limit=100
  /api/v10/channels/900001/messages?limit=50&before=900&limit=1&after=0
The provider-controlled id smuggled a duplicate `limit` and an injected `after` into the plugin's own paging query — on real Discord that silently returns a different window (or a 400), so the backward walk's contract ("a larger limit is not answered with a truncated head whose cursor already sits past everything older than it") is decided by response data rather than by the plugin.
remediation: `before === undefined ? \`limit=${size}\` : \`limit=${size}&before=${encodeURIComponent(before)}\`` — matching the `after=` arm one function below. Better still, build both query strings with `URLSearchParams` so neither arm can drift again, and tighten `hasUsableId` to require `/^\d+$/` (a Discord snowflake is decimal) so a non-routable id is refused at the seam boundary instead of at each interpolation site.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a provider-supplied string reaching a request URL without encoding. Widen `rest-contract.test.ts`'s 'a topic that tries to reshape the provider request' table from one axis (hostile TOPIC) to three (hostile topic × hostile CURSOR passed as `since` × hostile provider-returned `id` injected via `injectFault` on page 0 of a multi-page walk), and strengthen `expectStayedOnRoute`: its `CHANNEL_ROUTE` regex today ends in `(\?[^#]*)?$`, which accepts ANY query string, so it cannot see query injection at all. Assert instead that `new URLSearchParams(route.search)` has exactly the expected keys with exactly one value each, and that each decoded value equals what the plugin intended. Reuse the same HOSTILE_IDS strings ('x?limit=1', 'x&after=0', 'x#frag', 'x%2F') so the generator also covers inputs I did not try.

summary: `blockForMessage` arms a waiter, then calls `this.runFetch({...args, since: floor})`. Every settled exit is covered (`wake()` on a satisfied re-query, `await wait` on an empty one, `stop()`'s drain on disconnect, the socket-loss drain) EXCEPT a rejection: if the re-query throws — any `ok:false` that is not an absence code, a shape error, a repeated page cursor, a walk over MAX_HISTORY_PAGES — the exception unwinds past both `wake()` and `await wait`, so the waiter stays registered in `link.waiters` with a live timer, and every live event on that channel iterates it, until its own timer fires up to one ladder rung (≤5 s) later. `harness.ts`'s `parkedWaiters` doc names four exits and omits this fifth, and `withBlocking`'s guard only wraps calls that resolve.

Reproduced.
remediation: In the ladder body, wrap only the re-query so a throw drains its own waiter before propagating: `let requeried; try { requeried = await this.runFetch({ ...args, since: floor }); } catch (e) { wake(); throw e; }`. Use a catch, NOT a finally — a `finally { wake() }` would fire before `await wait` on the normal empty-page path and turn the capped ladder into a hot re-query spin.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a registered resource whose release is on the success path only'. Add REJECTION as an explicit exit axis to the blocking-fetch table: parameterize over {woken, timed out, disconnected mid-park, socket lost, re-query rejects} × {a 4xx-shaped ok:false, a SlackShapeError, a repeated page cursor} and assert `parkedWaiters(plugin) === 0` for every one, with the call captured via `capture()` so a rejection is a row failure rather than an unhandled rejection. summary: seam.ts states ascending-cursor handler invocation as a plugin guarantee, and src/link.ts's own class comment concedes the plugin suspends it during a `disconnect: warning` rotation ('it rests on ONE connection feeding a channel, which a rotation deliberately suspends'). During the grace both sockets are established and `routeEnvelope` invokes handlers from either — it never checks `this.ws === ws` for an `events_api` envelope — so for up to `rotation_grace_ms` (default 10 000 ms) the live path can deliver a channel's events out of ts order. The README's only mention of that window is the config comment 'how long a rotated-out socket may stay open once replaced', which describes a connection count, not a relaxed ordering guarantee. No test grades ordering across a rotation either: connection-lifecycle.test.ts's rotation rows assert socket counts and that the replacement carries the stream, never the order of what is delivered.
failure: Subscribe to a mapped topic, push `{type:'disconnect', reason:'warning'}`, wait for two live sockets, then have Slack route event ts=…002 to the replacement and ts=…001 to the still-open old socket. The handler is invoked with …002 before …001 — a descending pair on a seam that declares ascending order — and an operator reading the README has no way to predict it.
remediation: Document it: add a sentence to the README's rotation/`rotation_grace_ms` text stating that a rotation deliberately runs two connections for up to `rotation_grace_ms`, that Slack routes each payload to exactly one of them, and that live-path ordering is therefore not guaranteed inside that window — catch-up (`fetchRecent` cursor order) is the ordered path. The behavioural alternative — after the replacement greets, keep the old socket ACKING but stop invoking route handlers from it (gate the `events_api` arm of `routeEnvelope` on `this.ws === ws`) — restores single-source ordering but converts a gapless rotation into live-push loss for that window, repaired only on the next catch-up; do not take it without deciding that trade explicitly.

Add a rotation-ordering row to connection-lifecycle.test.ts driven from the fake's two-socket state: subscribe, push the warning, wait for `liveSockets===2`, then push a descending-ts pair across the two sockets and assert the handler order the package COMMITS to. Pair it with a README-parity test in the style of documented-scopes.test.ts — key the assertion off the exported `DEFAULT_ROTATION_GRACE_MS` and require the README paragraph to name both the constant and the ordering caveat — so a future relaxation of any other guarantee has to move the prose with it.

summary: `StoreFile.replace()` calls `writeSync(fd, text)` once and ignores the byte count it returns. `fs.writeSync` performs a single `write(2)` and does NOT loop (unlike `appendFileSync`/`writeFileSync`, whose looping this package already relies on — see store-torn-write.test.ts's own comment). A short write returns normally, so the code proceeds to `fsyncSync`, `closeSync` and `renameSync`, publishing a TRUNCATED file over the only copy of this backend's history. `writeOwn()` (line 115, the `.hw` mark) has the identical shape.
failure: Reproduced standalone: `StoreFile.replace(journal)` with a 46913-byte journal (400 records) under an 8192-byte write ceiling. `replace` threw NOTHING; the store file was published at 8192 bytes holding 71 whole records plus a torn fragment, not newline-terminated. On the next load the fragment is dropped, `#seq 400 400` states intact=400 against onDisk=71, so the store mints a fresh epoch and refuses every outstanding cursor — 329 observed messages gone, with no Bot API history endpoint that could put them back. README.md line 77 claims the opposite: "a crash or a full disk mid-compaction leaves the previous file intact rather than a truncated one".
remediation: Write the whole buffer or fail: in both `replace()` and `writeOwn()`, `const buf = Buffer.from(text, 'utf8'); let off = 0; while (off < buf.byteLength) { const n = writeSync(fd, buf, off, buf.byteLength - off); if (n <= 0) throw new Error(`ObservedStore: short write to '${path}'`); off += n; }`. The existing `catch` in `replace` already closes the fd, unlinks the temp and rethrows, so a filesystem that fills mid-rewrite then leaves the pre-compaction file untouched — exactly what the README promises.

In store-compaction.test.ts add a fourth `Interruption` — 'short write, no error' — whose `writeSync` mock writes `data.slice(0, data.length >> 1)` and RETURNS that count instead of throwing, asserting the same three invariants the existing rows assert (pre-compaction records all readable, store still appendable, fd still valid). Add a source lint over `src/**` that a bare `writeSync(` result is never discarded.

summary: `fetchOnce` calls `AbortSignal.timeout(budgetMs)` before the `try`, with no validation. Node requires an integer in [0, 4294967295], so a fractional or oversized budget throws a raw `RangeError` that bypasses the label/redact/sanitize envelope this module's own test file asserts nothing leaves without. `budgetMs` is `deadlineMs - (now() - started)`, so BOTH documented knobs reach it: `deadlineMs` (documented with no integer constraint) and `now` (documented only as "Injectable clock, for tests").
failure: Reproduced in-repo against the real module. `fetchWithRetry(url, {}, { label: 'L', isStopped: () => false, deadlineMs: 100.5 })` -> rejects with `RangeError: The value of "delay" is out of range. It must be an integer. Received 100.5` — no `L → ` prefix, no redaction of the credential-bearing URL, and `statusOf(err) === undefined`. Worse, `{ label:'L', isStopped:()=>false, now: () => performance.now() }` with the DEFAULT deadline -> `RangeError … Received 29999.994656` on the very first attempt, i.e. the obvious high-resolution reading of the documented `now` option makes every call fail. `deadlineMs: 5_000_000_000` -> `RangeError … must be >= 0 && <= 4294967295`. And `deadlineMs: 3_000_000_000` (under 2^32, over 2^31) is silently clamped by Node's timer to 1 ms with a `TimeoutOverflowWarning`, aborting the request immediately.
remediation: In `fetchWithRetry`, validate the caller's bounds once, up front, and reject inside the envelope: if `!Number.isFinite(opts.deadlineMs ?? DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS)` or it is <= 0, throw `new LabelledError(`${opts.label} → deadlineMs must be a positive finite number of milliseconds`, undefined)`. In `fetchOnce`, arm the signal from a normalized figure rather than the raw one: `AbortSignal.timeout(Math.min(Math.trunc(budgetMs), 2 ** 31 - 1))` — the truncation makes a sub-millisecond clock (`performance.now`) harmless, and the ceiling stops Node's 32-bit timer overflow turning a long deadline into an instant abort.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a caller-supplied bound reaches a Node API that validates it, outside the envelope": add a table in `fetch-with-retry-outcomes.test.ts` over `[deadlineMs, now]` pairs — `100.5`, `0.5`, `NaN`, `Infinity`, `-1`, `2**31`, `2**32+1`, `undefined` × `Date.now`, `() => performance.now()`, `() => 0.5` — asserting for every cell that the rejection message starts with `` `${label} → ` `` and that `err instanceof RangeError === false`. Widen it mechanically rather than by list: derive the option names from `declaredOptions()` (already parsed in `package-contract.test.ts`) so a future numeric option arrives as rows. The existing `honours the deadline against %s` rows are too narrow — every one passes an integer literal, and `now:` is only ever `(clock += 1)`.

In fetchOnce it relies on `const deadline = AbortSignal.timeout(budgetMs);` being the only unvalidated Node call on that path (the other timer, `sleepUnlessStopped`'s `setTimeout`, tolerates any number).

summary: `DOOMED_BODY_BYTES = MAX_ERROR_BODY * 4` is the cap on a body the caller will never see — the README sells it as "a hostile upstream cannot spend your RSS producing a 2 KB message however many times it repeats the status", and its JSDoc states a lower-bound invariant ("enough that MAX_ERROR_BODY chars of it survive sanitizeBody even when every character is four bytes of UTF-8"). Neither bound is graded. The only checks near it are a coarse `tookBytes < 8 MiB` slack and `rssGrowth < 32 MiB`, which tolerate a 250x widening, and a `message.length <= MAX_ERROR_BODY + 200` ceiling with no floor tied to the constant, which tolerates a 32x shrink.
failure: Mutated `const DOOMED_BODY_BYTES = MAX_ERROR_BODY * 1000;` (8 KiB -> 2 MiB, a 250x widening of the per-attempt memory a hostile 429-repeating upstream can command, times up to DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS=8 per call): all 911 tests in packages/bridge-net-util pass. Mutated the other way, `Math.ceil(MAX_ERROR_BODY / 8)` (8 KiB -> 256 B, which truncates every operator-facing error body to 256 bytes and breaks the constant's own stated UTF-8 invariant): all 911 tests pass again. The constant is free in both directions.
remediation: Export the doomed cap (or a `doomedBodyBytes()` accessor) from the module and assert both bounds directly: (a) a 4-byte-per-character body (astral emoji) served on a doomed status must still yield MAX_ERROR_BODY characters before the truncation marker — that pins the floor to the stated UTF-8 invariant; (b) `tookBytes` on a doomed status must be under a small ABSOLUTE figure (e.g. 64 KiB) rather than the 8 MiB socket-buffer slack — that pins the ceiling. Keep (b)'s figure absolute, not derived from the constant, per this package's own `no elapsed-time bound is stated in terms of the figure it grades` rule.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a shipped bound that no row pins in either direction" by extending the existing `every shipped default is graded on the path it governs` block: it already derives the exported numeric defaults from `api` and forces each to be classified. Add the symmetric obligation — every classified figure must be named by at least one assertion that goes red when the figure is halved AND when it is multiplied by 100 — and add the internal doomed cap to that vocabulary by exporting it. Parameterize the doomed-body table over character WIDTH (1-byte ASCII, 4-byte astral) as well as volume, so the UTF-8 invariant is a row rather than a comment.

summary: The README promises, unqualified, that "this package's tests fail on the day a *second* fork appears — by name where one collides with an export here, and by BEHAVIOUR otherwise: a module-level function that decides something about a loopback address without asking this package is a fork whatever it is called." The implementing scan (`classifiers()` -> `consumerPackageSources()` in test/consumers.ts) only visits packages whose `src/` names `@sharptrick/parley-net-util` in a MODULE position. `bridge-core` and `bridge-sqlite` do not, so they are exempt by construction — and `bridge-core` has a divergent loopback classifier today.
failure: `packages/bridge-core/src/auth/invariants.ts:13` declares `export const LOOPBACK_HOSTS = new Set(['127.0.0.1', 'localhost'])` and `packages/bridge-core/src/config-auth.ts:22` re-decides the same question with `url.hostname === '127.0.0.1' || url.hostname === 'localhost'`. Both answer differently from `isLoopbackHost`: this package treats `::1` and all of `127.0.0.0/8` as loopback, core treats `::1` as remote (deliberately — it must match the MCP SDK's `checkIssuerUrl`). Neither is reported by `no consumer decides a loopback host without asking this module`, and neither CAN be, because core is forbidden by the prime directive to import a sibling package — `test/consumers.ts:62-64` even records that core names this package only in a licence-gap list. So the guarantee the prose gives an npm reader about a security predicate does not hold repo-wide, and cannot be made to.
remediation: Narrow the prose to what the scan enforces and state the exemption as an architectural fact rather than an omission: "…this package's tests fail on the day a second fork appears IN A CONSUMER of this package — a package that does not import it (bridge-core, which the prime directive forbids from depending on a sibling, and bridge-sqlite, which speaks no network) is out of scope, and bridge-core keeps its own deliberately narrower loopback set to match the MCP SDK's issuer exemption." Do not widen the scan to non-consumers: that would report a fork the seam requires.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a README sentence whose scope is wider than the check behind it" by pinning the SCOPE, not the sentence: add a row asserting that the set of packages `classifiers()` can reach equals the set `consumerPackageSources()` returns, and a second row asserting the README paragraph that describes the fork scan names that same restriction (e.g. matches /consumer/i and does not match an unqualified /whatever it is called/ without it). Parameterize over the two scans (`forks`, `classifiers`) so the next behaviour scan added here inherits the obligation.

summary: `clampBackoff` is a published semver commitment with ZERO call sites anywhere in the repo. The exemption record in `package-contract.test.ts` justifies keeping it as "the applier of MAX_BACKOFF_MS, which three backends read and two document by name" — but `MAX_BACKOFF_MS` is imported only by three packages' TEST files, never by any `src/`, purely as an assertion bound. So a published function is kept alive by a constant that no production code reads, to serve a use case ("a backoff a plugin chose itself — a reconnect ladder, a poll interval") that has no instances, while the duplication it exists to retire is present and growing next door.
failure: `grep -rn 'MAX_BACKOFF_MS|clampBackoff' packages/*/src packages/*/test` outside this package returns: three TEST files importing `MAX_BACKOFF_MS` (bridge-discord/test/readme.test.ts, bridge-slack/test/documented-scopes.test.ts, bridge-zulip/test/rate-limit.test.ts) and two COMMENTS naming `clampBackoff` (bridge-zulip/src/wire.ts:114, bridge-matrix/test/rate-limit.fake.test.ts:16). No `src/` calls either. Meanwhile bridge-zulip/src/pacing.ts hand-rolls exactly the ladder clamp `clampBackoff` is documented for — `LOOP_BACKOFF_MIN_MS = 200`, `LOOP_BACKOFF_MAX_MS = 5000`, `BLOCKED_FETCH_RETRY_MAX_MS = 5000` — and bridge-zulip/src/wire.ts:114 carries a comment asserting the clamp lives in `clampBackoff` "rather than being re-implemented — and re-tuned — per backend", which is the opposite of what that package does.

summary: `HEADER_ROWS.flatMap(… PARSERS.map(…))` is a 22 × 6 = 132-cell product. On the four `'stop'` rows the parser axis reaches exactly one outcome — every branch asserts `state.calls === 1`, `waits === []` and the same deadline message — so 24 of those cells are near-copies that cannot independently fail. The sibling redaction file guards precisely this shape with its own `crosses an axis only where its own values reach different outcomes` row; this table has no such guard.
failure: Take `['delay-seconds past the deadline', () => ['60'], 60_000, 'stop']`. With `no parser`, hinted = 60000; with `a doubling parser`, hinted = 120000; with `a zero parser` / `a NaN parser` / `a negative parser` / `a clamping parser`, the parser contributes nothing and the header floor of 60000 stands alone. All six cells then take the identical `overDeadline` branch and assert the identical three facts — `reported >= requestedMs - 2_000` is satisfied at 60000 and at 120000 alike. Six cells, one graded outcome, four times over. No mutation of the parser dispatch can redden one without reddening the other five.
remediation: Split the table: cross PARSERS only with the `'retry'` rows (where a doubling parser genuinely raises the observed wait and a clamping one must NOT lower it — the property the axis exists for), and keep the `'stop'` rows on a single representative parser plus one dedicated row asserting that a parser CANNOT push a retryable hint over the deadline in one direction and cannot pull an over-deadline hint back under it in the other. That is 18 × 6 + 4 × 1 + 2 = 114 cells instead of 132, and every remaining cell can fail alone.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a parameterized axis that reaches one outcome for a subset of rows" by lifting the redaction file's non-vacuity row into a shared shape and applying it here: before the product, assert that for each `outcome` group the set of observed envelopes across PARSERS has size > 1 — mechanically, run one header row of each outcome through all six parsers, collect `err.message` plus the recorded `waits`, and require `new Set(...).size > 1` for the group the axis claims to discriminate. That makes an axis going inert a red row rather than a silently growing product, whatever the next table crosses.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `const hinted = header === undefined ? parsed : Math.max(header, parsed ?? 0);` and `const overDeadline = elapsed + wait > deadlineMs;` in fetchWithRetry — the claim that the parser cannot change the outcome on a stop row rests on `Math.max` being monotone, so a parser can only raise `wait`, and raising an already-over-deadline wait keeps it over. A parser that could LOWER the header floor would make the axis live again, which is exactly what the loop is built to forbid.

summary: One invariant - 'this package's test sources are inside a tsconfig that a CI step compiles' - is implemented FOUR times: generically for all thirteen workspaces in packages/conformance/test/repo-contract.test.ts ('every test source in the repo is inside a tsconfig some CI step compiles', with a synthetic-root negative control), then again by hand in packages/bridge-sqlite/test/typecheck-coverage.test.ts (60 lines), packages/bridge-xmpp/test/typecheck-coverage.test.ts (68 lines, near-identical), and a 'CI type-checks this package's test sources rather than skipping it' describe in packages/bridge-matrix/test/shipped-artifacts.test.ts. The three copies also shell out to `npx tsc -b` with 300s timeouts on every npm test. And they have DRIFTED in exactly the way that matters: xmpp's copy asserts pkg.scripts['typecheck:test'] exists, with the comment 'CI runs npm run typecheck:test --workspaces --if-present, which turns a MISSING script into a pass - so the script's existence is asserted here too'; sqlite's copy, otherwise a near-transcription, dropped that one assertion. bridge-sqlite is precisely the package whose script is named `typecheck`, not `typecheck:test`.
failure: The drift is invisible to every package-scoped reader. bridge-sqlite's suite passes while the assertion that would have flagged its own naming divergence is the one line missing from its copy; bridge-xmpp's suite passes while asserting, about itself only, the rule sqlite violates. Meanwhile the generic guard already covers all three, so the copies buy nothing except worst-case tsc timeout budget and three places to keep in sync. A fourth backend added tomorrow gets zero of the three and full coverage from the generic one - the tell that the three are redundant.
remediation: Delete packages/bridge-sqlite/test/typecheck-coverage.test.ts, packages/bridge-xmpp/test/typecheck-coverage.test.ts and the 'CI type-checks this package's test sources' describe in packages/bridge-matrix/test/shipped-artifacts.test.ts. The durable guard is a meta-assertion in packages/conformance: derive the set of test files whose body contains '--workspaces' or reads its own package.json scripts to validate CI wiring, and assert that set has at most one member outside packages/conformance - i.e. repo-scale guards live in one place. Pair it with the existing repo-contract row so that removing the three copies cannot silently remove coverage. Existing tests too narrow to have caught this: all three copies, by construction - each grades one package and none can see the other two.

summary: The KNOWN_FORKS registry is a genuinely good instrument, but it grades only the EXISTENCE of a fork, never its behaviour - so a recorded fork may silently diverge from the shared implementation forever, and two of its three rows record duplication the table itself calls costless. bridge-nats:delay and bridge-redis:delay are recorded with the reason 'a duplicate with no obstruction at all: importing delay from here is a one-line change in that package, which owns it' - a permanently-green entry whose stated remediation is one line (packages/bridge-nats/src/jetstream.ts:11 and packages/bridge-redis/src/read-loop.ts:21 are byte-equivalent to packages/bridge-net-util/src/timing.ts:2 modulo the resolver's parameter name). More seriously, bridge-discord:plaintextRemoteOrigin (packages/bridge-discord/src/creds.ts:37) fails in the OPPOSITE DIRECTION from the shared one, and the registry cannot tell.
failure: net-util's plaintext.ts classifies by an allowlist of SECURE schemes and its comment states the rule: 'Keep the set on the SECURE side, so that a scheme this classifier has never met ... is warned about rather than passed'; its own test table carries the row ['x-vendor-stream', true] to pin that direction. bridge-discord's recorded fork classifies by a DENYLIST - PLAINTEXT_SCHEMES = new Map([['http:', 'https://'], ['ws:', 'wss://']]) - so plaintextRemoteOrigin('x-vendor-stream://evil.example.com') returns undefined (no warning) where the shared one returns the origin. Input -> wrong output: backend_config.gateway_url = 'x-vendor-stream://evil.example.com' produces no SECURITY line from packages/bridge-discord/src/session.ts:60, while the identical value through net-util warns. Both registry rows still pass: forks() only checks the NAME collides, and classifiers() only checks a loopback literal is not decided locally - and discord's fork delegates isLoopbackHost, so it is exempt from that scan too.
remediation: Retire the two delay rows by changing one import line in packages/bridge-nats/src/jetstream.ts and packages/bridge-redis/src/read-loop.ts (both packages already depend on @sharptrick/parley-net-util). For the discord fork, do what its own recorded reason says retires it: widen net-util's plaintextRemoteOrigin to return { origin, secure } | undefined (or add a sibling secureSchemeFor(protocol)), delete packages/bridge-discord/src/creds.ts:37 and import the shared one - which also flips discord onto the fail-safe direction.
testUpgrade: CLASS = a recorded-debt registry that pins existence but not behaviour, so a fork may drift from the thing it forked. Add to plaintext-classifier.test.ts a row set that runs each RECORDED fork against the shared implementation's own parameter table: for bridge-discord:plaintextRemoteOrigin, import the fork and assert fork(url) === undefined iff plaintextRemoteOrigin(url) === undefined across the existing SCHEMES x HOSTS cross-product (a fork returning a richer type is compared on its undefined-ness, the security-relevant bit). Add a second row asserting that any KNOWN_FORKS entry whose recorded reason contains 'no obstruction' fails the table - a debt with no obstruction is not a debt, it is an unmade edit.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: packages/bridge-net-util/src/plaintext.ts plaintextRemoteOrigin's branch `if (SECURE_SCHEMES.has(protocol) || hostname === '' || isLoopbackHost(hostname)) return undefined;`, and the existing SCHEMES/HOSTS tables in plaintext-classifier.test.ts that already pin its direction.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: gateway_url: 'x-vendor-stream://evil.example.com' would now produce a SECURITY warning from bridge-discord that it does not today.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: packages/bridge-net-util/test/plaintext-classifier.test.ts 'every recorded fork still exists, so the table cannot outlive the debt' would fail once the forks are deleted without also removing their KNOWN_FORKS rows - that coupling is intended. I grepped packages/bridge-discord/test/*.ts for assertions on the fork's { origin, secure } shape; they assert on the warning STRING via plaintextCredentialRisks, which the widened shared return keeps buildable.

summary: The `rotating` WeakSet ('one rotation per socket') appears to be unreachable-as-necessary, dominated by the two conditions beside it. `reconnect()` is an async function whose `if (this.reconnecting) return; this.reconnecting = true;` prologue runs SYNCHRONOUSLY, so by the time `routeEnvelope`'s warning arm returns, `reconnecting` is already true — a burst of warnings in the same tick is stopped by `this.reconnecting`. And `reconnecting` only returns to false in `reconnect()`'s `finally`, which is reached after `ensureSocket()` succeeded, i.e. after `openSocket` has reassigned `this.ws` to the replacement — at which point a further warning on the old socket is stopped by `this.ws !== ws`. I removed the `rotating.has(ws)` term and the full 880-test suite stayed green, which is consistent with it grading nothing.
failure: Not a runtime failure. `src/link.ts:65` (the WeakSet field + its JSDoc) and the `|| this.rotating.has(ws)` term plus `this.rotating.add(ws)` can all be deleted with the suite green — a guard carried as coverage that no interleaving in the fixture can distinguish.
remediation: Either delete `rotating` (field, JSDoc, add, and the disjunct), or keep it and add the interleaving test that shows what it catches — a second `disconnect: warning` on the SAME socket during a window where `reconnecting` has already returned to false but `this.ws` is still that socket. If no such window can be constructed, that is the answer.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a defensive guard no fixture can reach'. Rather than a test per guard, add a mutation gate to the package's own discipline: for each named single-socket/single-owner guard in link.ts (`reconnecting`, `rotating`, `this.ws !== ws`, `helloSeen`, the `session()` checks in `openSocket`/`ensureSocket`), a table-driven envelope-injection test that drives the specific interleaving each one claims to stop — pushing warnings and closes at chosen points relative to the replacement's `hello` via `fake.setGreet` and `fake.onHit` — so a guard that cannot be reached fails the table by having no row rather than by being silently green.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `reconnect()`'s prologue in src/link.ts:282-283 (`if (this.reconnecting) return; this.reconnecting = true;` — synchronous, before any await) and `openSocket`'s `this.ws = ws` at src/link.ts:227, which is the only assignment to `this.ws` other than `stop()`'s clear.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: Deletion accepts a second `disconnect: warning` on a socket that is still `this.ws` while no reconnect owner exists — if such a state is reachable, that warning would start a second rotation of the same socket.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I ran the full 880-test suite with the `rotating.has(ws)` term removed and it was green; the two rotation tests (connection-lifecycle.test.ts:506 and :534) both push warnings sequentially, each landing on a NEW current socket, so neither exercises the term.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If `rotating` really is dominated, deleting it changes nothing at runtime and removes a line that reads as covered but is not. If it is NOT dominated — i.e. there is an interleaving I did not construct in which `reconnecting` is false while `this.ws === ws` after a rotation already started — deleting it reopens a second-rotation-per-socket path, which is why the remediation is stated as an either/or and this is marked PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The one I could not rule out: `reconnect()` returns (finally clears `reconnecting`) without `openSocket` having reassigned `this.ws`. That requires `ensureSocket()` to resolve off a memoized `wsReady` belonging to an older socket, which the warning arm's `this.wsReady = undefined` immediately before `reconnect()` appears to prevent — but I did not trace every path that can re-arm `wsReady` between those two statements.
